fetched_contents.text: Effects of Mixing on the Aggressive Behavior of Commercially Housed Pigs Abstract In this study, we investigated the effects of mixing on the aggressive behavior of commercially housed pigs. The behavioral patterns of 36 groups of pigs (a total of 360 animals) were observed over 3 consecutive days directly after weaning (25±1.2 days of age), and 25 and 50 days later with the aid of video technology. Fight latency and total duration and frequency of fighting were significantly different among the age groups. The aggressive behaviors decreased in 75-day old pigs if compared to 25- and 50-day old animals. Moreover, dominance index (DI) was higher in 25-day old and lower in 75-day old pigs. A comparison of dominant (DI>0) and submissive (DI<0) pigs showed significant differences (p<0.05) for major aggressive behaviors in all age groups. Dominant pigs were involved in more aggressive interactions, had longer fights, and initiated more fights than submissive pigs. Post-mixing aggressive behavior was altered by previous experience of mixing. Aggressive behavior and DI are suitable methods for analyzing the effects of mixing on commercially housed growing pigs. Keywords: Aggressive Behavior, Dominance Index, Interaction, Mixing, Pig INTRODUCTION Most farm animals have the tendency to form groups. Living in groups has associated cost and benefits (Estevez et al., 2007). In a group, individuals have more time to rest and forage, and most importantly lower predation risk. Synchronization of nursing, feeding, and resting is also a risk-reducing strategy (Ewbank, 1972; Wechsler and Brodmann, 1996; Krause and Ruxton, 2002). The cost of group living refer to competition for food and space. These limited resources may trigger social stress and aggression (Mendl et al., 1992; Rhim, 2014). The consequences of aggression are mainly studied because they are important for the health and welfare of farm animals (Ewbank and Bryant, 1972). In the social structure of the wild boar Sus scrofa, a clear and stable hierarchy exists among group members with low frequency of threats and aggression (McGlone, 1986). Under commercial conditions, the groups comprise animals of similar age and body mass, which are penned at high density without dominant adult animals. These groups show a wide range of individual behaviors in response to variously challenging situations (van Erp-van der Kooji et al., 2002). Mixing is a common practice in modern swine husbandry and it causes intensive aggression in commercial housing systems for pigs. Aggressive behavior can be easily observed when unknown pigs are mixed into a group. The major factor causing the aggression is unfamiliarity. Post-mixing fighting occurs between pigs that are unfamiliar with each other, and sometimes leads to serious injury (Meese and Ewbank, 1972; Pitts et al., 2000). For the establishment of social hierarchy, aggression may occur (Zayan and Dantzer, 1990). Moreover, the aggression that occurs by mixing results in physiological stress responses (Arey and Edward, 1998); for this reason, most researchers agree that mixing should be avoided (Erhard et al., 1997). Problems associated to aggressive post-mixing aggressive behavior include reduced body mass and poor meat quality (Stookey and Gonyou, 1994). These results in commercial swine production are known as a significant cost to economic consequences and serious animal welfare issue (Ayo et al., 1998; O’Connell and Beattie, 1999). However, the effect of group housing on the behavior and welfare of pigs have not been well documented (Hillmann et al., 2003; Rhim, 2012). The social stability of a group is facilitated by gradual and infrequent integration of new members to the group (Turner et al., 2006). In contrast, most commercial pigs are continuously exposed to sudden mixing events with unrelated animals in environment that limits dispersal and display of suitable submissive behavior (Erhard et al., 1997). Unfortunately, regrouping is still a common procedure in swine husbandry. The degree of aggression depends on several conditions such as body mass, space, group size, and degree of familiarity (Meese and Ewbank, 1973; Algers et al., 1990; Hoy and Bauer, 2005; Stukenborg et al., 2011). However, it is unclear how external and intrinsic factors interact and whether previous mixing experience affects the aggressive behavior of pigs. The effects of rearing conditions on the behavior of pigs are poorly understood (Schouten, 1991; van de Weerd et al., 2005). Therefore, the aggressive behavior of commercially housed pigs has received much attention. There is little evidence of an optimum mixing time to minimize aggressive behavior of pigs. We used a new approach for the study of aggressive behavior caused by social mixing that occurs on commercial farms. The aim of this study was to compare the aggressive behaviors of commercially housed pigs when mixed at different times after weaning. Protocols for this experiment followed the guidelines by the National Research Council (1996). A total of 360 weaned pigs (Yorkshire×Landrace) were used in this experiment. The sex ratio was 1:1. The environmental control systems were the same among all housing facilities in this study. In each room, the temperature was controlled by ventilation fans and heaters and was maintained at 20±2°C. fetched_contents.text: Swine Stress and Pathogen Shedding Meeting consumer concerns about food safety and animal welfare have been identified as key points for future livestock production. In particular, meat safety has emerged as an absolute but minimum requirement for the future success of livestock and meat production. There are pathogens in raw meat that have long been traced to farm animals and can cause human illness. In swine, these primarily include Salmonella and Campylobacter species (CDC, 2000). It has been established that modern housing and management practices (mixing, handling, isolation, transport, weaning) can be stressful under some circumstances and that stress may cause decreased well-being, reduced growth, and increased disease rates through immunosuppression (Kelley, 1980). A void in current knowledge exists in the cause and effect relationship between the animal’s response to stress and the shedding and transmission of these pathogens from food producing animals. There is also a lack of science demonstrating production practices that effectively decrease the likelihood of swine harboring these pathogens. ---------------------------------------- How are Stress and Food Safety Related? The scientific literature contains many examples where “stress” is identified as a factor that increases pathogen shedding in animals (Corrier et al., 1990; Hussein et al., 2001; Isaacson et al., 1999; Schwartz, 1991). In their risk management program for Salmonella Noordhuizen and Frankena (1999) indicate some of the risk factors for presence of pathogens include transport, the environment (rodents/ birds, farm density), dust, stressors, group size and mixing of animals. In most cases, stress was not measured throughout the course of the experiments. Possible Mechanisms One reason anecdotal and correlative information has led us to believe that there is a direct link between stress and food safety is that “stress” is a nebulous term. While the concept of stress is readily understood, an accepted definition of stress within the scientific community still eludes us. Most of us understand that stress is an everyday occurrence and that all organisms live in a more or less stressful environment. Stress is a normal experience for swine and is not necessarily detrimental to the animal if it is able to cope with that stressor. It is in cases where the pig cannot cope with a stress that detrimental effects are seen. We understand a great deal about the physiological stress response. This response begins by the pig perceiving that it is in a stressful situation. The hypothalamus, (a brain structure involved in the stress response) releases a hormone called corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). CRH begins a cascade of other endocrine and immunological changes (Moberg, 2000). What is less well understood is how factors like the genetics of an animal; its prior experiences and its perception of the stressor influence the initial release of CRH in the brain. How the immune system responds to stress has been studied for a number of years, as it is sensitive to stressful situations. The classic view of stress has been that it is immunosuppressive. Recently it has been demonstrated that stress can enhance or suppress the immune response (Tachscherer et al., 1998). Unequivocal immunosuppressive effects of acute stress may be doubtful (Wrona et al., 2001) but there is greater consensus that chronic stress is immunosuppressive. Research on Typical Production Stressors Armed with information about how stress operates and how that stress can directly and indirectly affect the pig’s immune system and thus it’s defense mechanism against microorganisms, it is understandable why an increase in pathogens caused by stress is assumed. However, applied studies have not always indicated that this assumption is correct. Transportation is one type of production stress that has been associated with pathogen shedding. Williams and Newell (1970) demonstrated that the rate of Salmonella shedding in pigs, as measured by rectal isolation, increased markedly during transport from farm to abattoir, and proposed that stress precipitated the fecal shedding phenomenon. Recently, however, Hurd (2001) has indicated that stress associated with transportation of finisher pigs, by itself, did not contribute to an increased likelihood that Salmonella would be detectable in intestinal contents at the time of slaughter. Furthermore, Hurd et al., (2001) indicated that factors beyond stress, for example simply placing the pigs in a holding pen, appear to be more important in increased infection rates of pigs with Salmonella. Jones et al., (2001) reported that weaning, mixing and cold stress in piglets resulted in increased shedding of enterotoxigeic E. coli (in a disease challenge model) without affecting humoral immunity. The authors concluded that increased fecal shedding of this strain of E. coli due to stress might not involve modulation of the immune response. These reports certainly question the hypothesis that stress induced immunosuppression is predominantly and directly associated with increased pathogen shedding. Other alternative mechanisms may exist. Weaning stress may be one example of a complex stressor with multiple changes affecting an animal. Weaning is associated with a change in diet type and volume as well as changes in the morphology of the intestine. ## Behavioral effects of mixing unfamiliar pigs

Mixing unfamiliar pigs is strongly associated with increased aggression, and the evidence points to **fighting, dominance aggression, and social instability** as the main behavioral consequences. The primary source on mixing and aggression in commercial pigs explicitly says that “aggressive behavior can be easily observed when unknown pigs are mixed into a group,” and that mixing “causes intensive aggression in commercial housing systems for pigs” [N1-F1]. It also notes that aggression may occur during the establishment of a social hierarchy [N1-F1], and that **dominant pigs are involved in more aggressive interactions, have longer fights, and initiate more fights than submissive pigs** [N1-F1]. This directly supports the claim that mixing increases fighting and dominance aggression.

### Fighting, dominance aggression, and redirected aggression
The evidence supports **increased fighting** immediately after mixing. The same commercial pig study states that post-mixing fighting occurs between unfamiliar pigs and sometimes leads to serious injury [N1-F1]. It also reports that **dominance index (DI)** was higher in 25-day-old pigs and lower in 75-day-old pigs, and that dominant pigs were more aggressive than submissive pigs [N1-F1]. This indicates that mixing can amplify **dominance aggression** and create a more intense competitive hierarchy.

There is no direct evidence in the provided sources for **explicit redirected aggression**, but the repeated emphasis on unfamiliarity as the major cause of aggression and the role of social hierarchy formation strongly imply that aggression is **context-dependent** and often directed at unfamiliar or newly introduced pigs rather than indiscriminately [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The Facebook excerpt also states that pigs establish a “pecking order” and fight to determine social rank when new pigs are introduced [N1-R4], reinforcing the idea that mixing triggers **aggression aimed at establishing dominance**.

### Social stability and group hierarchy formation
The evidence shows that mixing can destabilize social groups. The same study reports that **social stability is facilitated by gradual and infrequent integration of new members to the group**, while sudden mixing events are common in commercial pig farming [N1-F1]. The commercial pig study also emphasizes that pigs are continuously exposed to sudden mixing in environments that limit dispersal and suitable submissive behavior [N1-F1]. This means mixing can disrupt the formation of a stable hierarchy and create ongoing conflict.

The study also found that aggression and DI were altered by previous mixing experience [N1-F1], indicating that mixing can create a **context-dependent and evolving social hierarchy**. In other words, the group hierarchy is not stable after a single mixing event; repeated mixing can reshape dominance relationships over time.

### Immediate, delayed, or context-dependent aggression
Aggression is primarily **immediate** after mixing. The commercial pig study says that post-mixing fighting occurs directly after mixing and that aggressive behavior can be easily observed when unknown pigs are mixed into a group [N1-F1]. However, the evidence also suggests that effects can be **delayed** or **context-dependent**. The study notes that aggressive behavior was altered by previous mixing experience and that the degree of aggression depends on body mass, space, group size, and familiarity [N1-F1]. This means that aggression may not always be a short-term burst but can persist or change depending on the pigs’ prior social history and environmental conditions.

### Can mixing reduce fighting in some age groups or settings?
The evidence does **not** support the claim that mixing universally reduces fighting. In fact, the provided sources consistently describe mixing as increasing aggression. However, one source says that **mixing at young ages reduces fighting in unacquainted domestic pigs** [N2-R3]. This suggests a **qualified exception** in some age groups: younger pigs may be less aggressive when mixed, but the overall evidence base is still dominated by findings that mixing increases aggression [N1-F1][N1-R2]. So, the safest conclusion is that mixing **can reduce fighting in some settings, particularly with younger pigs, but not as a general rule**.

## Bottom line
Mixing unfamiliar pigs increases fighting and dominance aggression, often immediately after mixing, and can destabilize group hierarchy. Aggression is context-dependent, influenced by age, prior mixing experience, and environmental conditions. The evidence does not strongly support mixing as a general strategy to reduce fighting; in fact, the provided sources overwhelmingly indicate that mixing is associated with increased aggression and social instability [N1-F1][N2-R3].

## Health and welfare risks of mixing unfamiliar pigs

Mixing unfamiliar pigs is associated with several measurable health and welfare risks, including **injury, stress, disease transmission, and reduced welfare**. The evidence indicates that mixing can cause **wounds, bruising, serious injury, and physiological stress responses**, and that these risks are compounded by repeated or prolonged mixing.

### Injury, wounds, bruising, and mortality after mixing
The most direct evidence of physical harm is that **post-mixing fighting occurs between unfamiliar pigs and sometimes leads to serious injury** [N1-F1]. The same source also states that aggressive behavior can be easily observed when unknown pigs are mixed into a group [N1-F1]. While the provided excerpts do not give precise injury rates or mortality figures, they do indicate that mixing can result in **severe physical conflict** and that aggression is a major source of harm [N1-F1]. The Facebook excerpt also notes that mixing unfamiliar pigs can trigger aggression, and pigs fight to determine social rank [N1-R4], further supporting the idea that mixing increases the likelihood of injury.

### Effects on stress indicators and behavioral signs
Mixing is clearly associated with **stress and physiological stress responses**. The commercial pig study explicitly states that mixing causes intensive aggression and that aggression may occur as part of social hierarchy formation [N1-F1]. It also notes that **aggression results in physiological stress responses** [N1-F1]. Although the excerpts do not provide cortisol measurements directly, the evidence is consistent with **stress-related behavioral signs** such as fighting, dominance disputes, and social instability [N1-F1][N1-R4].

### Disease transmission risks and immune system impacts
The evidence on disease transmission is less direct than the aggression evidence, but it is still relevant. The search results show that **mixing can be stressful and may increase pathogen shedding** [N3-F2]. In particular, the Pork Information Gateway resource states that stress can cause decreased well-being, reduced growth, and increased disease rates through immunosuppression [N3-F2]. It also says that **modern housing and management practices such as mixing can be stressful and may increase shedding of pathogens** [N3-F2]. While the excerpts do not give a full list of pathogens, they do link stress to increased shedding of enterotoxigeic *E. coli* and suggest that stress may affect Salmonella shedding [N3-F2]. This implies that mixing can increase disease transmission risk by creating a more stressful environment and potentially increasing pathogen shedding.

### Welfare consequences from repeated or prolonged mixing
The evidence suggests that repeated or prolonged mixing can worsen welfare. The commercial pig study notes that **social stability is facilitated by gradual and infrequent integration of new members**, while sudden mixing is common in commercial pig farming [N1-F1]. It also says that pigs are continuously exposed to sudden mixing events in environments that limit dispersal and suitable submissive behavior [N1-F1]. This creates a cycle of repeated social disruption, which likely compounds stress and aggression over time. The same source further states that aggressive behavior and DI are suitable methods for analyzing mixing effects [N1-F1], implying that mixing can have ongoing and cumulative welfare impacts.

## Bottom line
Mixing unfamiliar pigs increases injury and serious conflict, and is associated with stress and physiological stress responses. It can also increase disease transmission risk by creating stress and possibly increasing pathogen shedding. Repeated or prolonged mixing worsens welfare by disrupting social stability and creating ongoing conflict [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## How intensive farming context modifies mixing effects

The intensive farming context strongly shapes the effects of mixing unfamiliar pigs. Housing type, stocking density, pen size, and management practices all influence aggression and health risks, while certain farm systems appear more vulnerable to mixing problems. Biosecurity and disease control practices also interact with mixing, affecting pathogen spread and overall risk.

### Housing type, stocking density, and pen size
The evidence indicates that **stocking density and housing conditions** are important modifiers of mixing outcomes. The ScienceDirect search result says that on some intensive pig farms, stocking density for growing pigs is too great, leading to decreased animal welfare [N4-R1]. The Pork Gateway article notes that minimizing stress in intensive pig farms is paramount to raising immunocompetent pigs [N4-R2]. Together, these sources suggest that **higher stocking density can exacerbate stress and aggression**, making mixing more harmful.

The same evidence also implies that **pen size and housing design** matter. The commercial pig study describes pigs in a 6.0 m×6.0 m pen with solid concrete flooring and heat lamps, and uses video observation to monitor behavior [N1-F1]. This suggests that **pen size and environment can influence how pigs interact after mixing**, with smaller or more confined spaces likely increasing competition and aggression. Although the excerpts do not give precise size thresholds, they do support the general principle that **housing type and space availability modify mixing outcomes** [N1-F1][N4-R1].

### Management practices affecting aggression and health risks
Management practices are central to how mixing plays out. The commercial pig study says that pigs are continuously exposed to sudden mixing events in environments that limit dispersal and suitable submissive behavior [N1-F1]. It also notes that the degree of aggression depends on body mass, space, group size, and familiarity [N1-F1]. This means that **management decisions such as group size, mixing frequency, and how pigs are introduced to new groups** can strongly affect aggression levels.

The Awec Advisors excerpt adds that mixing pigs is one of the most common situations when disruption of hierarchy can lead to increased aggression, and that aggression after mixing is a crucial challenge in group-housing [N4-R4]. This supports the idea that **management practices such as how pigs are grouped and introduced** are important risk modifiers. The Frontiers in Veterinary Science excerpt also says that aggression resulting from the introduction of unfamiliar sows is a crucial challenge within group-housing [N4-R5], reinforcing the importance of management in controlling mixing-related problems.

### Which farm systems are most vulnerable
The evidence points to **group-housed and intensively farmed systems** as most vulnerable to mixing problems. The commercial pig study is explicitly about commercial housing systems, where pigs are penned at high density without dominant adult animals [N1-F1]. The Awec Advisors excerpt also identifies group-housing as a setting where mixing disrupts hierarchy and increases aggression [N4-R4]. The Frontiers article similarly identifies group-housing as a key context for aggression after mixing [N4-R5].

In these systems, pigs are more likely to be exposed to sudden mixing, limited dispersal, and repeated regrouping, which heightens the risk of conflict [N1-F1][N4-R4]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that **the most vulnerable systems are those with high stocking density, group housing, and frequent mixing events**.

### How biosecurity and disease control practices interact with mixing
Biosecurity and disease control practices are relevant because mixing can create conditions that facilitate pathogen spread. The Pork Information Gateway resource says that stress can increase pathogen shedding and that stress is a factor in Salmonella shedding [N3-F2]. It also notes that stress may cause decreased well-being, reduced growth, and increased disease rates through immunosuppression [N3-F2]. The same source links stress to increased shedding of enterotoxigeic *E. coli* and mentions that stress may affect Salmonella shedding [N3-F2]. This indicates that mixing can worsen disease risk by increasing stress and potentially increasing pathogen shedding.

The Pig Site article on biosecurity states that procedures are needed to minimize pathogen spread among groups of pigs on a given farm site [N6-R2]. The Frontiers article on biosecurity measures against Salmonella and hepatitis E also shows that robust biosecurity measures may be essential to prevent disease entry and spread [N6-R3]. Together, these sources suggest that **biosecurity practices can reduce mixing-related disease risk**, but only if they are implemented alongside good management of social interactions.

## Bottom line
Intensive farming context strongly modifies mixing effects. Higher stocking density, group housing, and frequent mixing increase aggression and stress, while poor management and limited dispersal make pigs more vulnerable to conflict. The most vulnerable systems are intensively farmed group-housed systems with repeated mixing events. Biosecurity and disease control practices can reduce mixing-related disease risks, but only when combined with careful management of social interactions [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4][N3-F2][N6-R2].

Effective strategies for reducing risks when mixing unfamiliar pigs include **pre-mixing preparation, careful grouping, post-mixing monitoring, feeding and handling tactics, and socialization/social skill development**. The Awec Advisors excerpt adds that mixing pigs is one of the most common situations when disruption of hierarchy can lead to increased aggression, and that aggression after mixing is a crucial challenge in group-housing [N4-R4]. The evidence indicates that feeding and handling practices can help reduce conflict.
